prompt: A Kubernetes container works as root but fails as UID 10001 when writing a mounted volume. Lead diagnosis, safe restoration, and durable least-privilege prevention.
directAnswer: Treat root success as evidence that may bypass ordinary checks, not as the solution. Trace numeric identity from image and securityContext through every mounted path component, volume ownership/ACL, fsGroup behavior, mount flags, user namespaces, and LSM policy; then correct the narrow owning boundary.
foundation: The kernel compares numeric UIDs/GIDs and capabilities. Kubernetes can set runAsUser, runAsGroup, supplemental groups, fsGroup, privilege escalation, and filesystem policy. Volume plugins and user namespaces change which host-side identities and ownership operations are meaningful.
reasoningSteps: Bound affected workload, operation, volume, node, rollout cohort, data sensitivity, and customer impact; preserve the non-root failure.
Inspect image USER and entrypoint assumptions, then actual UID/GID/groups/capabilities inside the exact container.
Inspect pod/container securityContext, volume type, mount path/options, fsGroup and fsGroupChangePolicy, CSI behavior, and user namespace.
Trace numeric owner/mode/ACL and traversal at the storage authority; correlate AppArmor/SELinux and admission evidence.
Choose image-time ownership, storage provisioning, narrow group/ACL, or bounded init-time correction appropriate to the owner; do not recursively mutate shared data blindly.
Canary, verify required write and durable read-back, prove unauthorized denial, monitor latency/ownership drift, and retain rollback.
seniorAnswer: I would pause a security-context rollout if impact is growing and keep a failing replica for evidence when safe. Root success says discretionary privilege may mask the defect. I compare declared and actual numeric credentials, effective capabilities and no-new-privileges, then map the container path to its volume and inspect every component at the storage authority. I verify whether that CSI driver implements fsGroup and whether user-namespace or idmapped behavior changes host IDs. A durable fix gives the application only the operation it needs—predictable image/runtime IDs, provisioned group ownership, or a narrow ACL/policy. I reject runAsUser 0 and fleet-wide recursive chmod. The canary must write/read the real harmless operation, preserve existing data, and show another identity remains denied.
weakAnswer: Set runAsUser to 0 or chmod -R 777 on the volume.
whyWeak: Both bypass the intended control, expand blast radius, may corrupt or stall a shared volume, and leave identity ownership unresolved.

evidence.proves: The outcomes differ with runtime privilege/identity in the tested paths.
evidence.doesNotProve: Which discretionary, mount, namespace, capability, or LSM gate caused the difference.

evidence.signal: volume root is numeric 2000:3000 mode 0770 and container lacks group 3000
evidence.proves: Ordinary group-class access is unavailable to that container identity.
evidence.doesNotProve: That changing all ownership is safe or that ACL/LSM layers permit it.

evidence.proves: The Pod requests group handling semantics.
evidence.doesNotProve: That the volume driver applied them, the path was rewritten, or every existing object inherited access.

followUps.prompt: Why prefer numeric IDs in evidence?
followUps.answer: Names are local mappings; kernel and filesystem authorization compare numeric credentials, possibly translated through namespaces.

followUps.prompt: When is an init-container chown unsafe?
followUps.answer: On large/shared volumes it can be slow, race with other writers, cross ownership boundaries, mutate hard links or unexpected paths, and delay every rollout.
Identity and ownership are encoded at image, workload, storage-provisioning, or policy ownership layers and verified on new volumes and rollouts.

rubric.observableEvidence: Traces image, runtime, Kubernetes, namespace, volume, and storage numeric identities.
Avoids root/broad recursion, uses bounded canary and rollback, and preserves data.
Encodes ownership and proves positive and negative authorization outcomes.
